title: Visualizations and the questions they answer (preview)

blocks.content: Explore dashboards on Grafana Play one panel at a time to see what each visualization is for and the question it answers.
Open the **Sample Website Dashboard**.
Find the **Support calls** panel. It shows one large number, a stat.

This panel answers the question: What is the current value? Here, the value is the number of support calls. The faint line beneath the number sketches how the value moved, but the number is what the viewer takes in at a glance.
Focus on **Sign ups**, another stat panel.
This panel answers the same question for sign ups. The current value is the number of people who have signed up.
Next, focus on **server requests**, a time series panel.

This panel answers the question: How has this value gone up and down over time? Here, the value is the number of requests the server handles.

A stat would reduce those values to one number and hide the pattern. A stat suits a key metric to check at a glance. But when the viewer needs the trend, a time series says more.
Explore a gauge and a bar gauge to see how each one shows a value within a range.
Open the **Grafana Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory** gauge.

This panel answers the question: How close is the value to a limit? Here, the value is memory use. The filled arc shows where the value sits within a range, which a value-only stat doesn't show.

The range is the panel's min and max, 0 and 300 here.
Focus on the horizontal **Google hits** bar gauge.

This panel answers the same question for several values at once. Each bar's length shows its value's position within the range, a bar instead of an arc. Don't confuse it with a bar chart, which compares categories on a shared axis.
Explore a bar chart and a pie chart of the same counts to see how one compares categories and the other shows each part's share of a total.
Open the **Bar charts and pie charts** dashboard.
Find the **Popular JS Frameworks** bar chart.

This panel answers the question: How do the values for different categories compare with each other? Here, the categories are six JavaScript libraries, and the values are their GitHub stars, forks, and watchers.

Each color is a different count, so compare bars of one color. Here the bars follow the order of the data, not size, so the tallest isn't first. **React.js** comes before **Vue**, though Vue's **Github Stars** bar is taller. Read lengths, not positions, and hover over a bar to read its exact count. The counts measure different actions, not how many people use each library.
View the **Popular JS Frameworks** pie chart.

This panel answers the question: How much of the total does each part make up? Here, the total is the six libraries' combined stars, and each part is one library. **Vue**'s slice is larger than **React.js**'s because its star count is larger.

All six libraries' slices add to 100%. The whole is their combined star count, not all libraries, all developers, or all library usage. A pie fits here because those counts add up to a total, while the bar chart only showed which count is larger.
Explore a table to see what it lets you do that a chart doesn't.
Open the **Visualizing Google Sheets Data** dashboard on its **Advanced Examples 1** tab.
Find the **Top 50 Post Data** table.

This panel answers the question: What are the exact values, row by row? Here, the rows are the fifty most-viewed forum posts, with each one's replies, status, and last post date.

The column headings, **id**, **title**, **reply_count**, **views**, **last_posted_at**, **category_id**, and **status**, tell you what each cell holds. The post with the most **views** is at the top, with its **title**, **status**, and last post date in the same row.

Click the **reply_count** heading. The rows re-sort by that column, descending first and ascending on the next click. The post with the most replies is a different post from the one with the most views.

By sorting the status column, you can easily compare posts with the same **status**. A bar chart could show which bar is longer. Only the table gives you the exact numbers, with the title, date, and category beside them.
